tasks.q: Step through a linear search for 31. Tap each item the algorithm checks, in order.
tasks.fb: Four checks, because 31 is the fourth item. A linear search never skips ahead.
tasks.title: Linear search: find 31

tasks.q: Where does a linear search start?
a: At the first item in the list
tasks.fb: Always at the start, always one at a time.

tasks.q: What is the main advantage of a linear search?
a: It works on a list that is not in order
tasks.fb: Sorting a list first costs time a linear search doesn't need to spend.

tasks.q: Which of these suit a linear search? Select all that apply.
opts: A short list of names in no particular order
A list that changes every few seconds
A list of only a dozen items
A million sorted records searched constantly
correct: A short list of names in no particular order
A list that changes every few seconds
A list of only a dozen items
tasks.fb: Short, unsorted or constantly changing: linear wins on simplicity.

tasks.q: A list has 500 items. What is the worst case for a linear search?
tasks.fb: The worst case is the item being last, or not there at all.

tasks.q: Step through a linear search for 5, the last item. Count how many checks it takes.
tasks.fb: Seven checks: the worst case for a seven-item list.
tasks.title: Linear search: the worst case

tasks.q: A list grows from 1,000 to 2,000 items. What happens to the worst case?
tasks.fb: The work grows in step with the list, which is what makes it unsuitable for huge data.

tasks.q: Why do large systems sort their data?
a: So they can use a much faster search that needs the list in order
tasks.fb: That faster search is the binary search, next lesson.

tasks.q: Put these lines into a working linear search.
tasks.fb: Set the flag, check everything, report the flag.

tasks.q: Why is the flag set to false before the loop?
a: So that a list with no match still gives a sensible answer
tasks.fb: Without it the variable has no value if nothing matches.

tasks.q: Write a linear search. The program should say at which position a name is found, or that it is not there.
brief: The list is already written for you - do not change it.
Read one name from the user.
If the name is in the list, print the position it is at, counting from 0.
If it is not in the list, print: not found
tasks.starter:
names = ['Ava', 'Ben', 'Chi', 'Dev', 'Eve']

tests.why: Chi is the third name, and counting from 0 that is position 2.
The first item is at position 0, not 1.
The last item has to be checked too - a loop that stops early will miss it.

tasks.fb: Go through the list one at a time and compare. Remember the answer for a name that is never found.

tasks.q: Which is the strongest description of a linear search?
a: It compares the target with each item in turn from the start, stopping when it matches or the list ends
It searches until it finds it
tasks.fb: Starting point, what is compared, and when it stops.

tasks.q: A question asks how many items a linear search checks to find the fifth of eight items. What is the answer?
tasks.fb: Items one to five are compared.

tasks.q: Find 42 with a linear search. Tap each item the algorithm checks.
tasks.fb: Three checks: the algorithm stops as soon as it matches.
tasks.title: Linear search: find 42

tasks.q: Would a linear search be a sensible choice here?
items: Twelve names in no particular order
A shopping list on your phone
A list that is rebuilt every second
A dictionary searched thousands of times a second
Every web page on the internet
tasks.fb: Short, unsorted or rapidly changing suits linear; large and sorted does not.

info.title: Also called sequential
info.text: A linear search is sometimes called a sequential search, because it goes through the list in sequence.

info.title: Sometimes unbeatable
info.text: If the list is unsorted and you search it once, a linear search is the fastest possible: anything else would have to look at every item too.

info.title: Your eyes do it
info.text: Scanning a shelf for a particular book is a linear search, which is why bookshops sort their shelves.

info.title: Early exit
info.text: A well-written linear search stops the moment it finds a match, which halves the average work.

info.title: Big O
info.text: At A level this is written O(n): the work grows in proportion to the number of items.

info.title: Exam tip
info.text: Questions often ask for the number of comparisons. Count how many items are looked at, including the matching one.
